newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London ended slightly firmer but off the day's highs. March added $2.40 to close at $311.90 per tonne, while May was up $2.0 to close at $310.90 per tonne. Activity was mainly technical without fresh fundamental news. In New York raw sugar futures settled at a 10-week high on technically-driven trade. Early trade buying carried the most- active March contract through key-psychological resistance at 11.00 cents/lb. March added 14 points to close at 11.08 cents/lb, while May ended 13 points firmer at 11.07 cents/lb. This was a very bullish close and some traders are expecting further gains. However, fundamentals remain negative and the surplus this year is likely to cap any price rise. FUNDAMENTALS

UNITED STATES - President Bill Clinton has decided to extend the suspension of the lawsuit provision (Title Three) in the Helms-Burton law for a further six months. The legislation is designed to punish foreigners who do business on properties seized from Americans after the 1959 revolution. It has been widely condemned in the EU, which has made it the subject of a complaint in the World Trade Organization. Europe has adopted retaliatory legislation which would allow European companies punished under the law to sue for damages in European courts. Similar legislation came into force in Canada on January 1. Canada strongly opposes sanctions against the Castro regime. The Canadian trade minister, Art Eggleton, called the extended waiver on lawsuits under Helms-Burton 'disappointing'. 'It continues to be unacceptable behavior by the United States in foisting its foreign policy on to Canada,' he said. Cuban officials said the Helms-Burton law has had only a limited effect in dissuading foreign companies from investing in Cuba. Cuba's vice-president and economy minister, Jose Luis Rodriguez, said the number of ventures and deals involving foreign capital signed by Cuba had increased to 260 in 1996 from 212 in 1995. But the Helms-Burton act has forced some foreign companies to restructure their operations in Cuba to avoid the legal reach of the US law. Cuban sources pointed out that in spite of the renewed waiver of Title Three of Helms-Burton the law remains largely unchanged. Titles One and Two, which are clearly interfering in nature, and Title Four, which allows company executives to be punished, remain in place, Cuban sources said. Titles One and Two demanded radical political change in Cuba, while Title Four allowed the United States to bar from entry executives of foreign firms deemed to be doing business on expropriated property. This last provision was used against executives from a Canadian mining firm and a Mexican telecommunications company that invested in Cuba.

JAPAN - Sugar imports in November 1996 amounted to 168,176 tonnes, raw value, down from 201,988 tonnes in October 1996 and 199,700 tonnes in November 1995. This brought cumulative imports in the first two months of 1996/97 (October/November) up to 370,164 tonnes compared to 400,538 tonnes in October/November 1995. Total imports in 1995/96 reached 1.681 million tonnes against 1.716 million tonnes in 1994/95 and 1.704 million tonnes in 1993/94. Major countries of origin in October/November 1996 were Australia with 200,167 tonnes raws against 242,898 tonnes, South Africa with 91,095 tonnes compared to 84,442 tonnes and Thailand with 46,141 tonnes, down from 72,427 tonnes.

NEW ZEALAND - Sugar imports in November 1996 amounted to 19,109 tonnes, raw value, up from last year's 6,938 tonnes. This brought cumulative imports in the first eleven months of 1996 (January/November) up to 237,443 tonnes, sharply up on last year's 170,505 tonnes. Total imports in 1995 amounted to 210,379 tonnes compared to 215,117 tonnes in 1994. The major country of origin in January/November 1996 was Australia with 151,361 tonnes raws compared 137,177 tonnes and 78,486 tonnes whites against 29,350 tonnes. Sugar exports in January/November 1996 reached 18,873 tonnes, down from 19,849 tonnes the like period in 1995. Major countries of destination in 1996 were French Polynesia with 5,156 tonnes whites against 5,175 tonnes and New Caledonia with 4,393 tonnes compared to 4,426 tonnes.
